42198955a7.why: The order is now true. Shechtman hunted for twins on the afternoon of 8 April 1982 (NIST), and a Technion account says tests that day ruled twinning out. Pauling's twinning papers came in 1985 (Nature 317:512, cubic crystals) and 1987, and he held to the idea until 1994. 'Argued for years' and 'had already' carry that order, and the grade_note no longer says the test answered Pauling. The choices are two tenfold and two ordinary, the three lures being what twinning predicts. The key is the shortest and no longer echoes 'alone'. 'Already' gives the narrative only a faint lean, inherent to a what-did-the-test-show question; the stem never says who was right.

e8872f66ec.why: Fact true: 'New mitochondria and plastids are formed only through binary fission', and a cell whose mitochondria are removed cannot make new ones (Wikipedia, Symbiogenesis; Grokipedia, Mitochondrion: new ones come from fission of existing ones). The history in the context is accurate: Bell and Muhlethaler (J Cell Biol 1964, the fern Pteridium) suggested new mitochondria 'may be generated from the complex evaginations of the nucleus', so 'The nucleus pinches off new ones' is a fair plain rendering. Diers (J Cell Biol 1966, the liverwort Sphaerocarpus) found 'no indications' of it. Grade: fair at T4, since it applies T3 two-ways-to-make-offspring (bacteria grow and split; yeast buds) to Margulis's claim, and budding is the real confusion. The only known support for budding is one group's cryo-electron tomography, which it calls a 'new hypothesis'; that does not make the budding lure defensible against the textbook consensus. No other stem or context in the unit says how mitochondria multiply, and no other unit keys it.

Applying the T2 fact that chloroplasts make food from sunlight is fair at T4. The doubters' view (step by step inside the cell) stays in.

f997ddce6c.why: LEAD FIX applied (2026-11-27): the re-checker's exact sentence replaced in the context. Re-checker's note: The revision means to stop the context giving away 74c56090f0's key, and it does not fully do so. The stem says Bretz's flood was 'one huge, sudden flood'. The new context then says the water 'came from a vast lake in western Montana, held back by a dam of glacier ice', the very lake of 74c56090f0's stem. Together they tell a player that the lake emptied in a sudden flood, which is 74c56090f0's key ('The lake had emptied in a fast, deep rush'), and they kill its three lures. 74c56090f0's own context already teaches the source. Exact fix: replace the sentence 'It came from a vast lake in western Montana, held back by a dam of glacier ice, whose old shorelines Joseph Pardee of the US Geological Survey had traced.' with 'Without one, careful geologists had good reason to wait for more evidence.' That keeps the steel-man and also clears the fact-check's Pardee note. Otherwise sound: the key is documented (UChicago Magazine), the lures are wrong, and Penrose 1979 and the forty years are right.
